title: Ashoka's edicts
hookLine: carved in stone across India: honor other people's faiths as well as your own (Rock Edict 12)

lines: HOW TO SPEAK OF ANOTHER FAITH.
cards: No printing press, no screens, no post. How does a king talk to everyone at once? Ashoka chose rock.

He had his words cut into boulders and polished stone pillars where people passed, and some readers picture someone who could read reading them out to those who couldn't. The messages weren't lists of taxes.
They were about how to live. And one, the edict scholars number twelve, takes on a question that still starts arguments at dinner tables: how should people of one faith speak about another?

teach.b: First, written to last. The edicts speak in the king's own voice, Beloved of the Gods, and say plainly they were written so the teaching of dhamma would endure.
They're not scripture; they're a ruler's public letters about kindness, honesty and care. Second, the root.
Rock Edict Twelve says the king honors all the religious communities, wandering ascetics and householders, with gifts and respect.
But he values something more than gifts: that the essential part of every one of them should grow.

teach.h: RESTRAINT IN SPEECH IS THE ROOT.
teach.b: The root of that growth is restraint in speech. Don't praise your own community and run down another's without reason, and when there is reason, do it lightly. Third, the surprise.
Whoever praises their own faith and condemns another's, just to make their own look good, the edict says, does their own community more harm.

teach.h: RUNNING OTHERS DOWN HARMS YOUR OWN.
teach.b: Honoring the other faith helps your own; running it down injures it. Fourth, listening.
Concord is good, the edict says: people should hear one another's teaching and become well informed. The king wants communities that know each other, not just tolerate each other from a distance.

Buddhist tradition remembers Ashoka as a patron of the sangha, yet here, in public stone, he asks respect for every community in his lands. It's a king's instruction, and it reads like advice for a group chat.

how: Buddhists and historians point to Ashoka's twelfth rock edict as a public call for respect between religious communities.

o: a king's public messages, cut into rock and pillars
laws on taxes and trade, posted in the markets
sacred verses the Buddha spoke, written by monks

games.q: carved in stone: tap the pairs.
p: cut into rock and pillar to last
the root of growth, says edict twelve

s: edict twelve says the king honors all the religious communities, ascetics and householders alike.
the edict says praising your own faith by condemning another harms your own
running another down, it says, does your own community more harm.
the edicts were mostly tax lists
they speak about dhamma: kindness, honesty, care and restraint.

games.q: you're a king who loves one religious community. how do you tell your people to speak about the others?
o: praise yours and warn them about the rest.
honor them all, restrain your speech, and listen to each other.
say nothing about religion at all.
games.why: edict twelve honors every community, makes restraint in speech the root, and calls for people to hear one another's teaching.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose faith or way of seeing the world differs from yours, a coworker, a neighbor, a relative, and recall one thing about how they live it that you respect: a kindness, a discipline, the way they treat people.
If an urge to add a but shows up, let it go by. Then simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Ashoka's edicts. A king's words about how to live, cut into rock and pillar so they'd last.

orig.note: Prakrit and Pali: dhamma, the word the edicts use for the good way of living the king urged.

carryVoice: Your line: carved in stone. Honoring another's faith, the edict says, helps your own. See you tomorrow.
